ety.text: The noun is from Middle English joye, borrowed from Old French joie, from Late Latin gaudia, neuter plural (mistaken as feminine singular) of Latin gaudium (“joy”), from gaudēre (“to be glad, rejoice”). Doublet of jo and gaudy (“Oxford college reunion”). Displaced native Old English ġefēa. The interjection is from the noun. The verb is from Middle English joyen, joȝen, joien, from Old French jöir, from the Old French noun (see above).

senses.d: A feeling of extreme happiness or cheerfulness, especially related to the acquisition or expectation of something good.
ex: a child's joy on Christmas morning
It is his joy to walk in the rain.

senses.d: Anything that causes such a feeling.
ex: the joys and demands of parenthood
For, ye are our glory and ioy.

senses.d: Luck or success; a positive outcome.
ex: Grant had no joy with taking a nap, so he began to systematically feel if everything was working: fingers and toes, etc.
'Rob? It's Gary. Are you having any joy with this trip to Bali?' 'No joy at all, mate. I reckon Bali's out for the foreseeable future. […]

senses.d: The sign or exhibition of joy; gaiety; merriment; festivity.
ex: Such ioy made Vna, when her knight she found;
'Joy! joy!' he cried, throwing his arms towards Heaven, 'on a grave be the site of our Temple; and now our happiness is for Eternity!'
I joy to see you wear around your neck the holy relic I bestowed on you;—but what Moorish charmlet is that you wear beside it?
I haue my wish, in that I ioy thy sight,

For from the time that Scudamour her bought,
In perilous fight, she neuer ioyed day […].

senses.d: To give joy to; to congratulate.
ex: Then round our Death-bed ev'ry Friend ſhou'd run, / And joy us of our Conqueſt, early won: […]

senses.d: To gladden; to make joyful; to exhilarate.
ex:
Yet neither pleasure’s art can joy my spirits,
Nor yet the other’s distance comfort me.

ety.text: Inherited from Old French joie, from Vulgar Latin or Late Latin *gaudia, from Classical Latin gaudium.
Borrowed from Old French joie, from Late Latin gaudia, from Classical Latin gaudium. Doublet of gaudio. Cognate with Sicilian gioja.
Borrowed from Latin fēlīcitātem. By surface analysis, felice + -ità.
Inherited from Old Spanish gozo, from Latin gaudium.
